detail:
StatPearls' vasovagal episode chapter describes reflex syncope as a failure of blood pressure autoregulation that drops cerebral perfusion pressure until consciousness is briefly lost. Vasovagal syncope is the most common form, accounting for more than 85% of syncopal events in people under 40, with a lifetime incidence above 33%. Triggers include pain, emotional upset, medical settings, and prolonged standing, though sometimes no trigger is found.

Diagnosis rests mainly on the story of the episode, including its warning symptoms such as diaphoresis, warmth, nausea, and pallor, supported by an ECG, orthostatic measurements, and tilt table testing in selected cases. The evaluation's central job is separating this generally benign faint from cardiac causes of syncope, which carry a very different risk.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about any fainting episode.
summary: StatPearls describes vasovagal syncope as the most common form of reflex syncope: a brief loss of consciousness when blood pressure regulation falters, often triggered by pain, emotion, or standing, and often preceded by nausea, warmth, and sweating.
takeaways: more than a third of people have a vasovagal episode in their lifetime
warning signs often include nausea, pallor, and sweating
evaluation rules out heart causes of fainting
tell your doctor about every faint, especially one without warning signs
title: Vasovagal syncope: the most common faint
